title: The most annoying aspect of AI-assisted game development is that nobody talks about how hard, expensive, time-consuming and long it still takes to develop high-quality games, even with the best AI tools available
author: Post-reality
selftext: It's so annoying that the image of AI game developers is of a few prompts-here-is-the-game image. I have been working on my title since September 29th. It's a game I have been dreaming about for over 20 years. In the past (prior to recent AI tools) I begged my software engineer brother to develop it for me, and eventually even planned to just a hire game studio to develop it for me. Now that I can develop it myself, it has been a blast, working 18 hours everyday, 7 days a week, using and experimenting with all kind of frontier models (for voice, music, animation, sprites, etc). But reading about hoq people view AI game developers as if they just prompt a game into existence..... Yeah those would produce tech demos, or just re-skinned concepts of existing games, not new games. Currently, AI can't read minds, and it's a terrible designer (looking at you, Claude). It's a form of a jagged intelligence - brilliant in some aspects, while being dumb in others. Creating good games still take months, if not years. Also, tokens/credits are quite expensive, especially for assets (visual design, dialogue, animation, sound efftcts, layers). At the current rate, it may take me over a year to finish my game. If not for AI, it would have costed tens of millions of dollars to develop. Yet, AI is merely a human augmention tool, not a human replacement. We have been automating aoftware development for decades (from low-level languages to high-level languages, from custom engines to modular game engines, from manually writing code to using boilerplates and copying code from Google and OverStack Flow, from creating assets and logic from scratch to libraries, frameworks, and pre-made assets, from using notepads to IDE's) - AI is just a new productivity tool; or another layer of abstraction in other words.

replies.author: Post-reality
replies.body:
The last time that I took interest in hiring a game studio a few years ago, I took into account that:

1) I can hire a small "discount" studio who you share post-production sales/profits with.
2) That the industry matured and developed internal tools which can let you replace a lot of the hard labour (using pre-made game engine, networking solution, backend, etc).
3) only developing a modular prototype which I can later "mod" it myself manually.
4) Dumbing down the passion or cutting corners.

All of that would have brought down the game development costs to tens of thousands of dollars in the best scenario, if not hundreds of thousand of dollars.

As for the current project project, I take into account development costs from 20 years ago, and the current scope (which is much higher than originally thought). Imagine a flashy game with complex physics and ech character has hundreds of poses/sprites and on top of that thousands of pieces of layers (lower body, upper body, legs, head, etc) - back in the day, studios would have just xut corners (minimizing number of sprites, customizion comes in full gear piece - if not a combination of them). Now adds vocal dialogue, facial expressions, animating all kinds of in-game scenarios...... I am not aware of anyone developing something as complex when it comes to 2D animation compared to what I'm doing.

replies.author: Post-reality
replies.body: "I think it has the weakest merits of many AI arguments" - quite the opposite, it's the most sounding now, if you aware of history and how raising labour productivity works like. Mario was once an AAA masterpiece, or Half-Life 2 was in its own release time - those games are completely outdated by today's standards. If you think AI is going to democratise game development, then you are in for a rude awakening. AAA companies are going to be the biggest beneficiers as they have the budgets, manpower and resources for buying tokens and utilizing them effectively. It's just that AAA games, 10 years from now, will be much more complicated, with photorealistic graphics, complex physics, large open-world maps, procedurally generated content and NPCs using AI agent (the ability to affect the world, NPCs with their own lives, stories and lores). For the same reason our cars, smartphones and houses get more and more complicated each year.

replies.author: Ohgood9002
replies.body:
What game, and what is the mod? Have you decompiled the iso? 3 weeks is still a long time for a mod unless its a full overhaul. I am curious about what you're trying to do and why its taken 3 weeks.

Just yesterday I added jedi academy style directional based combat and a system for a grappling hook based off of the just cause series. Two incredibly complex systems, especially when it comes to physics. I didnt copy and paste the code. I told my agents to decompile study and research the code and then use what it learns to write our own engine code from the ground up

That was done in a day. Yeah it can use a little more polish but if i can do that in a day, and you're struggling with a ps1 mod I have to wonder what the approach you're taking is. Or if your mod is really more of an overhaul instead of adding or changing a mechanic

replies.author: Scrample2121

Speed is not my goal, quality is. I can get it done, but will it be done well? 

I'm adding 100's of new Digimon to Digimon World 1, new cutscenes, new maps, new attacks, etc.

I've had to rewrite a lot of the game to make this work and keep it potentially playable on a PS1 still which is one of my dream goals.

Each digimon needs tested in game for model errors, all animations, noises, etc. Hundreds of hours just running around in game to make sure it looks right. A lot of these are huge fan favorites and if I don't do them to the best of my ability I will let a lot of people down.

comments.author: Standard-Struggle723
comments.body:
As someone who's been on both sides of development, it's more annoying that the socio-economic narrative is just obliterating any insightful discussion about the potential uses for the technology to begin with across and in each domain that it's touching. Which gives me the feeling that it seems the vocal minority of people don't have any interest in understanding how to use AI as a tool, and are more concerned about being perceived as ethically superior in the struggle against the economic boot it's being represented as. This in turn is making everyone socially and intellectually reclusive online because no one wants to deal with mob-mentality brigadeering, or AI psychosis nutjobs who can't have a normal discussion about it to begin with. What I think is a real concern is that it's becoming harder to find intellectually similar people to have thoughtful discussions with.  
  
Personally I've been working on my project for about 2 years now, I started out doing everything myself on many of the available game engines and then leaving that space to begin developing my own engine and networking architecture to make running networked games as cheap as possible at any scale with a very specific rendering aesthetic, I've since transitioned into AI assisted development and suddenly people where were my peers in the graphics rendering, game design, architecture space are now no longer viable contacts simply because I'm now using AI to overcome my shortcomings and assist me in learning far faster than I would have on my own.   
   
My professional background is Infrastructure Solutions Architect, my bachelors and masters thesis was about MMO scale architecture engineering. I'm not a gas station clerk suddenly using AI and masquerading as a professional and yet I get treated like I am because the results of my project don't match the time I invested vs the "professionals" in the field. The gatekeeping, bitching, and blacklisting is unreal.

I think the perception that AI use is low effort only because they themselves either don't have access to the same tools, can't make it work the same way, are jealous or do have access but perceive themselves capable of interfacing with it in the same way and at the same level as someone who has more advanced knowledge or skills without actually attempting to learn or gain good enough skills, it's like saying everything made with Blender is blender slop because it makes art creation easier than manually coding the vertices of polygons by hand. Literally Perfect Dunning-Kruger fueled by ego.

The wider social commentary problem I see stems from the information asymmetry required to make viral social media posts compounded by the fact that opening up any frontier AI tool environment and getting something that looks complete but isn't is far less burdensome than opening up, again, something like Blender and immediately getting confused, lost, and disheartened because the interface is arcane enough to keep laymen from intuitively using it. Now that AI can kind of do a lot of things and seemingly offload a ton of the burden and mutli-domain dependancy it just makes it harder for people to realize the massive knowledge, domain specific expertise, language, intuition, foresight, and critical thinking skills required for actually good use of AI unless they really try to attempt it themselves and fail miserably.  
  
Then again on the developer side you either get steamrolled by egotistical programmers that only care about how a thing is written rather than the objective of the sum solution. Or you go to r/godot and see people celebrating laughably small wishlist counts of some garbage they tried to piece together and then cry posting after launch wondering why it didn't equate to financial success, or you just watch the ThreeJS html centric space freak out over web browser rendering and tout the amount of times people clicked a link you start wondering if the internet is just a bunch of 13 year olds who have no marketable skills or careers to begin with and all think they are going to hit big with their special ideas. 

Maybe I'm just poisoned to it all because my opinion of people I used to respect is dropping into the fucking black hole of anti-intellectual tribalism and I can't find people to talk to that see the results and concepts as more important than the process.  

Thanks for listening to the rant.

comments.body: Couldn't agree more. People think ai is magic when it's really just a helper you have to guide 24/7. Making a good game takes real design vision and feel that only humans have. If you let ai take over the design, what's the point of making the game?

comments.author: Disastrous-Gain5870
comments.body: Yep, it still takes an incredible amount of work. It’s just sped up a bit, but for one person it’s still a massive undertaking if you’re making a semi-expansive game of any sort.

comments.author: trai1er_dude
comments.body: There's a big problem with your premise; you cannot solely develop high quality games with AI, it can help but the main factor is the developer if you don't have the experience, which most people using AI to create games don't, then it's just going to be slop.

comments.author: maikoo811
comments.body: Agreed. I’m full-time on mine too, weekends included, and honestly working with a human team was easier. My eyesight has gotten noticeably worse these past few months. AI gets you to average. Getting what I actually want takes forever. Design especially, I’m bouncing between AI tools and each one has its own quirks, so briefing it, getting something back, explaining what’s off, going again, it’s the same loop I’d have with a designer. Easier with a human, but I can do it alone and fast this way.
